item.title: Announcing Peaseblossom: an Oberon-2 compiler, and libraries and programs for it and for voc
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
This software was developed with the aid of AI.

I'm announcing a set of Oberon-2 projects: a compiler, libraries, and programs built with them. All are on GitHub, and the software is under the BSD 3-Clause License.

For voc (Vishap Oberon)

  • olibfyaml: a binding to libfyaml, the YAML 1.2 parser and emitter. It covers parsing, navigation, typed values, building and emitting YAML or JSON, anchors, tags and source locations. Errors in the input come back as values with file:line:column messages.

For both voc and poc

  • opp: the Oberon pretty printer. It reformats modules within a maximum line length and keeps every comment. It handles both compilers' language extensions. Before writing, it checks that its output has exactly the tokens and comments of its input.

  • Ropes: ropes, strings represented as trees of pieces, with a self-test and a command-line demo.

  • ArgParser: command-line parsing: long and short options, clustered short options, option values, commands, and usage messages.

Peaseblossom

  • poc, the Peaseblossom Oberon Compiler: an Oberon-2 compiler with an LLVM backend for Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD, and a VAX backend for VAX/VMS 5.5-2. It was motivated in large part by my wish for a more modern language than the limited ones available on the VAX system I maintain. A release tarball needs only clang and GNU make, or it can be bootstrapped using Vishap Oberon. Packages are available for Fedora, Debian, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD. It comes with a User's Guide and a Reference Guide.

  • polibfyaml: olibfyaml for poc, with the same API, tests and examples.

    • ova_fmt_po, an example program using polibfyaml: it formats characters for the OVA tabletop RPG from YAML as reStructuredText, gemtext, Markdown and more.

  • pofltk: a thick binding to FLTK 1.4. FLTK's classes are record types a program extends, and draw() and handle() are type-bound procedures it overrides. Coverage includes widgets, layout (flex and grid), menus, dialogs, text editors, browsers, trees, tables, images, the clipboard and preferences. FlTest drives a program's windows in tests on Xvfb or a headless compositor. Many of FLTK's test programs are ported as examples.

    • ova_cg_po, an example program using pofltk: a character generator for OVA. It's a complete program with a menu bar, tabs, grids, file choosers, preferences and window tests. Its tour for pofltk readers says where in its code each technique is.

  • poDateTime: dates, times, durations and time zones. It has instants, the proleptic Gregorian calendar, clocks, POSIX TZ rules and tz database files, ISO 8601, RFC 3339 and strftime formats. It runs on the four Unixes and on VAX/VMS.

  • pounix: Unix services that poc's runtime doesn't provide: dropping root for good, file descriptors and directories, running child processes with an argument list (no shell), and errno.

  • posockets: TCP (IPv4 and IPv6) and Unix-domain sockets. It works with poc's cooperative Tasks, so one thread can serve many connections, with deadlines.

  • polibtls: a binding to libtls (LibreTLS on Linux, FreeBSD and NetBSD; OpenBSD's own). It supports server contexts with several key pairs, client certificates, and non-blocking I/O with Tasks. It's tested against openssl, gnutls-cli and Go's TLS.

  • pogemini: a Gemini server built on the four libraries above. It serves several capsules by host name, each with its own certificate, and can require client certificates for parts of a capsule. Every connection runs in a task in one thread.

  • poDB: a database-independent SQL interface, with drivers for SQLite and PostgreSQL. A program moves from one to the other by changing its connection URL and the driver it imports.

Comments, bug reports and patches are welcome. Many of the poc libraries are early in their lives; polibfyaml and pofltk have had the most use.

item.title: Making digest-sized pages with pandoc and ms output
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
Note

After I wrote this post, I made a last minute check of the options to pandoc and found that the --pdf-engine-opt= option does exactly what I want. How embarrassing. So I changed this post, showing both the easy way and the hard way to do it.

I use pandoc to produce digest-sized pages (5½×8½ inches) in PDF documents from ReStructuredText. I have a ms output template, digest2.ms in ~/pandoc/templates that sets the page width and page height correctly. Unfortunately, there is no way to set the papersize properly in the template. [1]

Luckily, pandoc has the --pdf-engine-opt= option to pass options to the PDF engine that pandoc is using, in this case pdfroff. In the case of ms output the thing to do is pass the argument --pdf-engine-opt=-P-p8.5i,5.5i [2], like below.

GNUmakefile.pandoc-digest-pdf-engine-opt (Source)

%.digest.ms.pdf : %.rst
        pandoc -s -r rst -w ms --template=digest2 $(VARIABLES) \
                --output=$@ --pdf-engine-opt=-P-p8.5i,5.5i $<

Unfortunately when I originally had this need for digest pages I hadn't realized that the --pdf-engine-opt= option existed.

So I used pandoc --verbose and found the pdfroff invocation pandoc uses, and made my pandoc invocation output ms instead of PDF, then passed it through a pdfroff command with the added -P-p8.5i,5.5i argument. Here's what I put in my GNUmakefile:

GNUmakefile.pandoc-digest-save-ms (Source)

%.digest.ms.pdf : %.rst
        pandoc -s -r rst -w ms -s --template=digest2 $(VARIABLES) \
               --output=$*.ms $<
        pdfroff -ms -mpdfmark -e -t -k -KUTF-8 --no-toc-relocation \
                -P-p8.5i,5.5i $*.ms > $@

Or, if you don't care about having the ms output for debugging, you could do it as a pipeline:

GNUmakefile.pandoc-digest-pipeline (Source)

%.digest.ms.pdf : %.rst
        pandoc -s -r rst -w ms -s --template=digest2 $(VARIABLES) \
               --output=- $< | \
        pdfroff -ms -mpdfmark -e -t -k -KUTF-8 --no-toc-relocation \
                -P-p8.5i,5.5i - >$@

There are still some instances where this technique of having pandoc output the ms source directly and pass it through pdfroff yourself. For instance, if you have to do some massaging of the ms source, like changing .RS/.RE to .QS/.QE to get around the problem with block quotes in ms output in the current pandoc release, discussed here.

[1]

Heirloom Troff (originally at H1, but now I think more up to date at H2 and H3) has the .mediasize and .papersize commands for that.

[2]

Amusingly, pandoc passes the --pdf-engine-opt=-P-p8.5i,5.5i argument to pdfroff, which passes the -P-p8.5i,5.5i part to groff, which passes the -p8.5i,5.5i part to the (final) post processor — I'm not sure if that is grops or gropdf.

item.title: Video Chatting with P.B. and L.B
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description: I worked through setting up Google+ on my computer this evening with P.B., and then got worked through setting it up on L.B.'s phone, and got to video chat with her a good bit. It really made my day.

item.title: PDF-XChange Viewer
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
I like to stick to Free/Libre (as in freedom) and Open Source Software as much as I can, but I haven't found a open source program that lets me add text on existing PDF documents yet, so I use a commercial but free (as in costs nothing for personal use) program PDF-XChange Viewer, which can be downloaded here.

Unlike most of the other commercial but free programs that allow you to add text to existing documents, PDF-XChange Viewer doesn't add any nagware watermarking to the document to indicate that it was produced with the free version, so you can use it fill out forms in PDF documents that don't have electric form fields, which is very useful on long forms.

It's not perfect — I've had trouble with it on a few PDFs that seemed to have pathological defects — but overall it works well.

I'd still rather have a Free/Libre or Open Source program, though.

item.title: Case-insenstive filename completion with bash and emacs
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
It's strange, I know, that while I like case sensitive filenames, I don't actually want to be bothered matching the case exactly when I'm using tab completion. Fortunately, emacs and bash both accommodate my whims. For bash, add

set completion-ignore-case on

to your ~/.inputrc file. For emacs, add

(read-file-name-completion-ignore-case t)

to your emacs initialization files. Of course, if want to get rid of all completion case sensitivity, you need

(setq completion-ignore-case t)

too.

item.title: Updating NetBSD pkgsrc: swig checks for mcs
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description: It turns out that if you are upgrading your pkgsrc packages in a sandbox you really need to make sure that the home directory of the user you are using exists in the sandbox, if you use any packages that have a file:configure script that checks for mcs, since mono hangs if it can't use the home directory. Ugh.

item.title: Mousing in Emacs under Screen
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description: It turns out that if you execute the command xterm-mouse-mode (or evaluate (xterm-mouse-mode 1) in your initialization file) when running Emacs under Screen it allows “non-modified single clicks” to work. Normal mouse functionality is still available by holding the Shift key while clicking. I use the PuTTY ssh client for remote access to various servers, and this works well Emacs in Screen under PuTTY, too.

item.title: µstr - Micro String API - for C
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
I was very pleased to discover large parts of µstr compile and seem to work under VMS v5.5-2 with GCC 2.7.1, which is almost the only compiler available to me on that machine. The other is VAX BASIC, which has adequate simple string handling, but lacks advanced string handling and has only very painful facilities for dynamically allocating complex data structures and working with them.

[2019-11-09: I was writing a program to get e-mails from VMS Mail using the callable interface, then parse the body of the email into a form that could be further processed by POISE DMS programs.]

item.title: 2GB Windows XP Hibernation Problem
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
Coding Horror points out the hotfix for the:

⚠ Windows - System Error
Insufficient system resources exist to complete the API.

error when trying to suspend a Windows XP machine with 2 gibibytes. The hotfix is hosted by Owen Cutajar and is from Microsoft KB909095.

Update: 2008-12-11: Unfortunately, it doesn't always work. Even after applying the hotfix, one of my laptops still won't hibernate.

item.title: Cygwin setup crashes updating bash
item.dc:creator: T. Kurt Bond
item.description:
Thanks to the wonders of Google and Ruben I finally found the answer: remove (you'll want to make a backup copy before you remove it, though) /etc/setup/bash.lst.gz which apparently had become corrupted.

According to a comment on that post, running gunzip -t on all files in /etc/setup will tell you which setup files have been corrupted.
